name: Become invulnerable
summary: For a few moments the unit, or a teammate it protects, cannot be hurt: hits miss, pass through or do nothing. Something always pays for it: while protected the unit can't fire, move or hold objectives; it is slowed, unpowered or exposed afterwards; or it waits out a long recharge. Versions shield the user, one partner through a link, or allies in an area; some only stop the target from dying; and in one form the protection comes with the attack itself, so the unit is untouchable for each attack run or flurry, and the run leaves it slowed and exposed. The answer is always to wait it out, keep clear of what it can still do and punish the end. A barrier that soaks a set amount is raise-shield, taking less damage is brace, and locking a target out of the fight is lock-in-stasis.
counterplay: Stop wasting fire and wait it out: back off, reposition and save your burst for the moment it ends; many versions can't be ended early, so the timing is known.
Silence or stun it before it starts: a silenced unit can't turn untouchable at all.
Push, pull or hold it: knockback still moves a protected unit, and surrounding it keeps it in place until the protection fades.
Break the link or the device: kill or push away the teammate who gives the protection, or shoot the device that makes the field.
Dodge what it can still do: a protected attacker still has to hit you, so spread out and keep moving, then punish its slow, exposed way home.
Take the objective: in most shooters protected units can't capture or carry, so use the window to play the objective.

other_examples.note: A superweapon power that makes every vehicle and building in a small area invulnerable for a short time. Terror drones can't latch onto the protected vehicles, but mind control still takes them, and any soldier caught in the field dies, so it doubles as a weapon against infantry; building one warns every player and reveals the device. In the first Red Alert it covered one vehicle at a time (the manual also names buildings, but the wiki's ability text and trivia say structures cannot be targeted), on a very long recharge, and killed infantry riding in a protected transport.

sources.title: Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 manual, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Copies the game's printed manual (official text); read for the Iron Curtain entry.

sources.title: Iron Curtain (Red Alert 1), Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: The first game's version: one target, recharge time, infantry in transports; also says the Red Alert 2 version covers more units and kills infantry caught in its area.

other_examples.note: The expansion gives every side a defensive power that starts charging once a Battle Lab is placed. Used on one or more friendly buildings, an ally's included, it makes them immune to all damage, even from superweapons; the price is that the user's whole base goes without power for a short time.

sources.title: Command & Conquer: Red Alert 2 - Yuri's Revenge manual, Command & Conquer Wiki
sources.note: Copies the expansion's printed manual (official text); read for the Force Shield entry.

other_examples.note: A hero spell that shields the Paladin against every attack and spell for a fixed number of seconds; the duration and the cooldown both grow with each level, and since patch 1.17 he can't end it early. Enemies can't attack him while it lasts and must turn to other targets, which breaks focus fire. The usual answers are to silence him before he casts it, to run until it fades, or to surround him so he can't slip away and kill him when it ends.

sources.title: Paladin (Warcraft III), Warcraft Wiki
sources.note: Divine Shield ability box, counters and patch changes.

other_examples.note: An ultimate on a long cooldown that ties the protection to an attack: he leaps to a chosen enemy, then slashes it and other enemies nearby in quick succession for a few seconds, invulnerable and unselectable the whole time. It ends early when no visible enemy is left within reach, and it can't jump to invisible units or into the fog, so spreading out or going invisible can cut it short.

On a short cooldown he marks every enemy in a chosen circle, each shown by a flaming sword above it, darts from one to the next striking each once, and then returns to where he started. He is invulnerable and can't be selected throughout; enemies who walk into the circle after the cast are left alone.

sources.title: Ember Spirit, Dota 2 Wiki
sources.note: Sleight of Fist ability box and notes.

other_examples.note: Cast on an ally, who cannot die for a few seconds: hits still land and their side effects still apply, but health stops at a sliver, and healing on the ally grows stronger the lower its health. A halo over the ally sinks as the time runs out and touches the ground when it ends, and a few effects that kill below a health threshold still work.

sources.title: Dazzle, Dota 2 Wiki
sources.note: Shallow Grave ability box and notes.

shooter_analogues.note: The Medic fills a meter by healing teammates; once it is full he releases it, and he and the teammate on his beam turn shiny and can't be hurt for several seconds, but only while the beam stays on them, so it ends early if he dies, is pushed out of range or switches target. Knockback and the Pyro's airblast still move them, protected players don't count toward capturing points or pushing the cart (though they can block a capture) and can't pick up the intelligence, and a voice line when the meter fills warns the enemy.

A drink that makes the Scout invulnerable for several seconds, but he can't attack or switch weapons meanwhile, and hits only show a miss sign. He can't carry the intelligence or capture or defend points while it lasts, knockback still moves him, burning and bleeding pause until it ends, and afterwards he is slowed for a few seconds, the more so the more damage he soaked. The next can is ready after a cooldown.

sources.title: Bonk! Atomic Punch, Official TF2 Wiki

shooter_analogues.note: She encases herself in ice for up to a few seconds: she ignores damage, sheds most status effects and heals, but can't move or use abilities, and she can break out early; the cooldown starts when the ice is gone. The block stops line of sight both ways, so her own healers can't reach her until she comes out.

The player locks in place for a few seconds, immune to damage but unable to move; rockets glance off, vehicles that ram the player are damaged, and anyone who melees the shell is briefly stunned. On release it sends out an electromagnetic pulse that grows the longer the lock was held, and the player stays untouchable for a fraction of a second while stepping out. The standard answer is to wait outside the pulse and time a grenade to burst as the lock ends; a later update made heavy incoming fire drain the lock faster.

The pilot slips into another dimension for a couple of seconds, invisible and unharmable, free to move, reload and switch weapons but unable to heal or to see enemies who stayed behind; a ghost image marks where the pilot went in, and phasing drops a carried flag. At launch it had two charges and allowed healing; it was later cut to one charge with no healing.

A thrown device makes a small field for a few seconds in which his team's health can't fall below a quarter, so they can be hurt but not killed; anyone already lower is topped up to that floor on entering. The device has its own health and can be shot or hacked to end the field early, and terrain can block the throw.

An ultimate that turns the untouchable window into an attack: he leaps high out of the fight, where neither team can see or target him and he can't contest objectives, heals while he steers a target circle across the ground, then slams down after a short wind-up, hurting enemies in the circle (most at the centre) and slowing them.

He turns into a shadow for up to a few seconds on a short cooldown: he moves faster, takes no damage and sheds most status effects, but can't shoot or use his other abilities until it ends, and pressing the key again ends it early. His shotguns are reloaded to full, and a few area holds can still pin him in place, though they neither hurt him nor end the form.

After a wind-up of about a second, during which she is slowed, she steps into the void for a few seconds: she takes no damage, moves faster and can still see enemies, but can't use her weapons, doors or objects that abilities placed. Other players see a faint trail where she goes, there is a short pause on the way in and out when she can do nothing else, and a silence that lands before the wind-up ends stops it. The wiki's advice is to use it at about half health rather than as a last-moment save.

player_translation.summary: A short, loud window in which nothing can hurt the unit or the teammate it protects, paid for up front or afterwards: no firing, no moving, no objectives, a slump or a long recharge. It wins a fight by surviving a burst, carrying a push or landing a strike; the enemy wins it back by waiting out the window and punishing the end.
as_user: Press Q at the right moment: when the enemy commits its burst, to cross a deadly stretch, or to buy the seconds your teammates need to arrive.

Know the price: in the base version you move but can't fire or hold objectives and are slowed afterwards; in the frozen shell you heal but can't move; in the phase-out you move fast but can't touch anything.
Timing matters: too early wastes it, too late and you are already dead, and some versions have a short wind-up so it can't be a last-instant save.
With an ally version you make one teammate, or allies in a small field, untouchable for a push: stay close, keep the link up, and land the push before it ends.
With the attack-run version every attack is a commitment: nothing aimed can stop your run, but once the payload is away you are slow and exposed until you get home to rearm.
as_target: A protected unit wears a shiny shell in its team's colour with a ring that empties, and your hits show sparks and no damage, so you know at once to stop wasting fire.
Back off, reposition and save your burst for the moment the ring runs out.
What still works: knockback and pulls move it, a root or a body-block holds it, and a silence before it starts stops it.
Against a linked protection, kill or push away the giver; against a field, shoot the device.
Against an attack run you can't stop the strike: move out of the marked area, then catch the attacker on its slow way back.
teammates: A support with the linked version decides a push: one teammate becomes untouchable while the pair stays together, as Team Fortress 2's Medic shows.
The protected unit draws attention: enemies switch targets or hold fire, which frees the rest of its team.
The other team keeps a silence, a stun or a knockback for the start or the end of the window and times its burst for the end.
An attack-run bomber needs fighters or anti-air teammates to cover its slow way home, and the enemy's anti-air waits for exactly that moment.
controls: Q: become untouchable for a few seconds, on a long recharge; one counted key. The base version can't be ended early; the frozen shell ends early on a second press.
Linked-guardian variant: the healing beam on right mouse fills a meter, and Q pours the protection into you and the teammate on your beam while the beam holds.
Can't-die variant: Q throws the device that makes the field, or casts the protection on the teammate under the cursor.
Attack-run variant: no key of its own; every attack order on left mouse starts a run, so the protection is part of the weapon.
The universal keys work as on every unit.
feedback: A shiny shell or glow in team colour on the protected unit and a ring that empties, with start and end sounds loud enough to carry across a fight.
Hits on a protected unit show sparks and a no-damage mark instead of damage numbers.
A short wind-up glow before it starts, so enemies holding a silence or a stun can react.
Linked versions draw the beam between giver and receiver; fields show their edge on the ground and the device's health bar.
The attack run shows a sonic streak and a marker on the strike area a moment before the payload lands, then an exposed marker over the slowed attacker.
changes_from_rts: In the RTS the Aurora's immunity comes automatically with every attack order, and computer gunners aim behind it and miss; for a player the run stays tied to the attack, but it needs a loud streak and a strike marker, and the release must be clear so ground players know when to shoot back.
Keep the Generals rule that a wide blast bursting right beside the plane still hurts it, so splash anti-air keeps a job, and keep the slow, exposed return as the price of each run.

RTS invulnerability powers cover areas from a base building (the Iron Curtain, the Force Shield); a player version is short, personal or for one partner, on a recharge long enough to be a real decision.
Shooter versions stop protected units from capturing, carrying or pushing objectives, as Team Fortress 2 does; otherwise invulnerability wins objective games on its own.
Knockback, pulls and holds still work on a protected unit, so the enemy always has an answer, as airblast has against the Über.
The window opens and closes on the server's clock with lag compensation, so a shot fired just before the shell appears is judged fairly.

team_play.notes: The ally versions put a support player in charge of a push (the Über), the protected unit soaks the enemy's attention, and the enemy team must keep a silence, a stun or a knockback for the start or the end of the window; an attack-run bomber needs fighters to cover its slow way home.

notes: Every damage source must check one protected flag, damage over time included (paused or dropped), along with environmental kills and fall damage.
One rule table for what still works on a protected unit: knockback, pulls, holds, mind control, objectives.
Linked and field versions need a beam or a device with its own health, and a clear end when the link breaks.
The attack-run version ties the protected window to the weapon's attack state: commit, release, a short grace, then a slow return to a rearm pad.
Server authority: the window opens and closes on the server's clock with lag compensation, so shots fired just before it are judged fairly.
Invulnerability removes counterplay: on a short recharge or with a long window it makes a unit nearly unkillable.
Protection that still lets the unit attack (Omnislash, the Aurora's run, the Über's patient) is the strongest form; keep it short and costly.
Objective games break if protected units can capture or carry.
Stacking with healing (Mei heals inside her ice) or with other protection gives far more effective health than the price allows.
Shots that do nothing frustrate unless the shell, the miss marks and the timer are obvious.
Players must tell can't be hurt from can't die (Shallow Grave, Immortality Field): the second still takes hits.
For the attack run, the untouchable window and its end must show clearly, or ground players waste fire or miss the moment to shoot back.
Several protected units in one fight blur together; one consistent look per state helps.

variants.name: Untouchable shell
variants.summary: For a few seconds nothing hurts the unit; it can still move but can't fire, carry or capture, it can't end the shell early, and afterwards it is slowed, the more so the more damage it soaked, before a long recharge.
variants.seen_in: Team Fortress 2 Bonk! Atomic Punch; Warcraft III Paladin's Divine Shield (no early end)

variants.name: Frozen shell
variants.summary: Encase yourself: no moving, firing or abilities, but nothing hurts you and you heal and shed status effects; you can break out early, and the shell blocks sight both ways, so healers can't reach you either.

variants.name: Lock and pulse
variants.summary: Lock in place, immune and unable to move; melee attackers are stunned and rammers hurt, and releasing sends out a pulse that grows the longer you held, pushing enemies back, with a fraction of a second of protection as you step out.

variants.name: Phase out
variants.summary: Slip out of reach for a moment: faster or unseen, untouchable and free to slip through enemy lines, but unable to fire, heal or touch objectives; a ghost image or a trail shows where you went in, and a silence before it starts stops it.
variants.seen_in: Titanfall 2 Phase Shift, Overwatch Reaper's Wraith Form, Apex Legends Wraith's Into the Void

variants.name: Linked guardian
variants.summary: A healer fills a meter by healing, then makes itself and the teammate on its beam untouchable for several seconds, only while the beam holds; both can still be knocked about, neither can capture or carry objectives, and the ready call warns the enemy.

variants.name: Can't die
variants.summary: Allies in a small field, or one chosen ally, can be hurt but can't die for a few seconds, because health stops at a floor; a thrown device makes the field and can be shot, and a halo over a single ally counts down the time left.
variants.seen_in: Overwatch Baptiste's Immortality Field; Dota 2 Dazzle's Shallow Grave

adds_strengths.why: Keeps teammates in a small area from dying for a few seconds, which can turn a lost fight around.

adds_weaknesses.why: The field comes from a device that can be shot, and when the floor ends, hurt allies fall to the next burst.

variants.name: Protective curtain
variants.summary: A power on a long recharge covers allied vehicles and buildings in a small area, which can't be hurt for a short time; soldiers caught in it die, or the user's base loses power for a while.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 2 Iron Curtain; Yuri's Revenge Force Shield; the first Red Alert's Iron Curtain (one vehicle)

counters.why: Soldiers caught in the curtain die, so it doubles as a weapon against infantry, as Red Alert 2's Iron Curtain does.
Protected vehicles can't be latched onto: Red Alert 2's Iron Curtain keeps terror drones off.

variants.name: Untouchable attack run
variants.summary: No key: every attack run makes the unit untouchable to aimed fire, from the moment it commits until a moment after it releases its payload; direct shots miss it, but a wide blast bursting right beside it still hurts. Once the payload is away it slows down and must fly home to rearm, open to every anti-air weapon.
variants.seen_in: Command & Conquer: Generals Aurora Bomber's supersonic attack

adds_strengths.why: Once it commits to an attack run, aimed fire can't stop it, so its payload almost always lands.

adds_weaknesses.why: After each run it slows down and must fly back to rearm, open to anti-air and fighters the whole way.

countered_by.why: Anti-air can't stop the run, but kills the slowed plane as it turns for home.
Fighters catch it on its slow way back to rearm.
A wide blast going off right beside it still hurts it during the run.

variants.name: Untouchable flurry
variants.summary: Leap to an enemy and strike it and those around it in quick succession, untouchable until the flurry ends; it stops early when no visible enemy is in reach, and one version returns the striker to where it started. A leap out of the fight that ends in a slam on a chosen circle works the same way.
variants.seen_in: Dota 2 Juggernaut's Omnislash and Ember Spirit's Sleight of Fist; Overwatch Doomfist's Meteor Strike

adds_strengths.why: Strikes a group of enemies one after another while nothing can hurt it.

adds_weaknesses.why: Once started it is committed and its protection ends with it: it finishes beside its last target, back where it began or on the circle it chose; the Omnislash-style flurry stops early when no visible enemy is in reach; and the strongest versions then wait out a long recharge or an ultimate's charge.

adds_strengths.why: For a few seconds nothing can hurt it, so it rides out a burst, crosses a deadly gap or keeps a push alive.

adds_weaknesses.why: While protected it can't fire, move freely or hold objectives in most versions, and it pays afterwards with a slump or a long recharge.

counters.why: A bombardment's warning gives it time to turn untouchable before the strike lands.

countered_by.why: Silenced before it starts, it can't turn untouchable at all: the usual answer to Warcraft III's Divine Shield.
Knockback still moves a protected unit, pushing it out of position or away from its protector, as airblast does to Team Fortress 2's Über.

open_questions: Can a protected unit capture, carry or hold objectives? (Recommended: no, as in Team Fortress 2; it may block a capture but never score.)
Should knockback, pulls, roots and body-blocking still work on a protected unit? (Recommended: yes, so the enemy always has an answer.)

For the attack run: fully untouchable, or only to aimed fire, with a wide blast beside it still hurting it as in Generals? (Recommended: aimed shots miss and splash still hurts, so splash anti-air has a job.)
May a protected unit deal damage? The versions that can (Omnislash, the Aurora's run, the Über's patient) need a short window, a clear tell and a heavy cost afterwards; should they be T3 only?

This file puts the linked guardian (an ultimate charged by healing) and the protective curtain at T3, while the can't-die version, including its one-ally form, stays at T2 on a plain recharge. Should all the ally versions be T3?

shooter_fit.reason: Shooters already use it well (Team Fortress 2's Über, Overwatch's Cryo-Freeze, Halo's Armor Lock) and a shiny shell reads well from above; but every protected second takes away the enemy's agency, so it must stay short, costed, objective-proof and still pushable.
